domains.name: Vendor Landscape
domains.summary: How to map vendors to the problems they actually solve, translate marketing claims into verifiable specifications, price total cost of ownership, and avoid lock-in through portability and contract terms. Neutral evaluation framework; no vendor is endorsed and none is disparaged — the course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: Military-Grade Encryption
scenarios.situation: A vendor's datasheet claims 'military-grade encryption' for their SaaS product. Your procurement team asks what to verify before signing.
scenarios.prompt: How should you evaluate the claim?
evidence: The phrase
'Military-grade' is marketing language, not a standard or certification — it appears on products ranging from AES-256 systems to obfuscated proprietary ciphers.
What matters
Data is protected by specific algorithms, protocols, and key management: cipher and mode at rest, TLS version in transit, and who holds the keys.
choices: Ask for the actual specification — e.g., AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2+ in transit, and who holds the keys (you, the vendor, or shared) — because 'military-grade' certifies nothing.
Accept the claim; military-grade is an official certification tier.
Ask which general's office certified the product.
Encryption details do not matter as long as the user interface is polished.
scenarios.why: Security claims must resolve to verifiable primitives: named ciphers, protocol versions, and key custody. A vendor unwilling or unable to name them is selling adjectives. Key management is the sharpest question — encryption you cannot control the keys for is access control by another name.
scenarios.hint: Replace the adjective with a question: which algorithm, which protocol version, whose keys?

scenarios.title: Which Tool for the Problem?
scenarios.situation: You need to detect and respond to malware on employee laptops. One vendor pitches their SIEM; another pitches their EDR. Both demos look impressive.
scenarios.prompt: Which capability actually matches the problem?
evidence: Tool roles
EDR: detects and responds to threats on endpoints — process trees, isolation, remediation. SIEM: aggregates and correlates logs across many sources. Firewall: controls network traffic.
The gap
A SIEM with no endpoint telemetry is blind to what happens on the laptop; EDR without centralized logging leaves no cross-source correlation.
choices: EDR for detection and response on the laptops themselves; a SIEM aggregates logs across sources and answers a different question — buy the capability that matches the problem, then feed EDR telemetry into centralized logging.
Buy the SIEM; it automatically covers endpoints with no agents needed.
A host firewall on each laptop is equivalent to EDR.
Pick whichever vendor gave the better demo.
scenarios.why: Vendor mapping starts from the problem, not the pitch: endpoint behavior needs endpoint instrumentation. Demos optimize for impressiveness, not fit — the right question is always 'what data does this tool see that my problem requires?'
scenarios.hint: Ask what each tool can observe: which one sees process execution on the laptop?

scenarios.title: The Export Button Is Missing
scenarios.situation: Your ticketing SaaS holds five years of history. At renewal you discover there is no bulk export and no API — leaving would mean abandoning the data. The vendor offers a 'generous' renewal discount to stay.
scenarios.prompt: What is the lesson, and what do you negotiate now?
evidence: Lock-in levers
Data gravity, proprietary formats, missing exports, and contract terms that punish exit are the standard lock-in toolkit — in SaaS, your own data is the most common hostage.
The leverage moment
Leverage peaks before signature and at renewal; after signing, the vendor has no reason to grant portability.
choices: Treat data portability as a first-class requirement: demand documented export formats, API access, and a termination-assistance clause as a condition of renewal — and make portability a scored criterion in every future evaluation.
Stay forever; migration is impossible so there is nothing to negotiate.
Screenshots of old tickets are an acceptable export format.
Lock-in only matters for infrastructure, not SaaS.
scenarios.why: Switching cost is set at purchase time, not at exit time. Portability requirements — formats, APIs, assistance periods, timelines — must be contractual before you are dependent. The discount is priced against your inability to leave; negotiate the exit while you still can.
scenarios.hint: Ask when your negotiating power over this vendor will ever be higher than it is right now.

scenarios.title: Nines, Nines, and Credits
scenarios.situation: A vendor offers a 99.9% uptime SLA with service credits. Your buyer reads it as a promise of essentially zero downtime.
scenarios.prompt: How should you read the SLA?
evidence: The math
99.9% uptime per month allows about 43.8 minutes of downtime; 99.99% allows about 4.4 minutes. Credits typically refund a fraction of fees — not your lost revenue.
The fine print
SLAs exclude scheduled maintenance, force majeure, and often the very dependencies the product runs on; claiming credits usually requires you to detect, document, and file.
choices: Do the nines math, read the exclusions, and treat the SLA as a compensation schedule — then measure real reliability from status history and your own error budgets instead of the SLA number.
99.9% means at most one outage ever; the vendor guarantees it.
Service credits make downtime free, so reliability does not matter.
The SLA percentage is the only reliability metric worth tracking.
scenarios.why: An SLA prices failure; it does not prevent it. Forty-three minutes a month of allowed downtime, minus exclusions, minus a claims process you must operate — that is the actual offer. Real reliability judgment comes from observed incident history and whether the architecture (multi-AZ, status transparency) supports the claim.
scenarios.hint: Convert 99.9% into minutes per month, then ask who pays for your losses during those minutes.

scenarios.title: The Egress Invoice
scenarios.situation: After moving analytics to the cloud, the first bill shows data-egress charges dwarfing compute. The architects had modeled only the sticker price of instances and storage.
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the cost model?
evidence: Pricing dimensions
Cloud bills combine compute, storage tiers, request/API operations, and data transfer — ingress is commonly free while egress to the internet is metered, and each dimension scales differently.
The design flaw
The architecture pulls large datasets across region and internet boundaries repeatedly — the costliest possible data path, chosen by default.
choices: Rebuild the TCO model with all dimensions — egress, storage tiers, request costs, committed-use discounts — keep hot data near compute, tier cold data down, and compare three-year totals before re-architecting.
Egress fees are illegitimate; dispute the invoice and change nothing.
Move everything back on-premises immediately without analysis.
Delete historical data to cut the bill.
scenarios.why: The sticker price is never the total price: data movement, API requests, and premium tiers compound silently. Cost engineering means modeling the workload's actual access patterns against every pricing dimension, then designing data locality (regions, tiers, caching) to match — before signing commits or migrating back.
scenarios.hint: List every way the workload touches the meter — not just the servers, but the bytes moving between them.

scenarios.title: AI-Powered Everything
scenarios.situation: A vendor rebrands their rules engine as 'AI-powered' with no technical detail. Your team must decide whether the claim changes the evaluation.
scenarios.prompt: What due diligence pierces the label?
evidence: The rebrand
The product, pricing, and architecture are unchanged from last year's 'advanced heuristics' datasheet — only the adjectives moved.
What would matter
A real capability claim can answer: what model, trained on what data, evaluated how, with what failure modes and what human oversight.
choices: Demand specifics: what the model does, what data it trained on, how it is evaluated (precision/recall, benchmarks against baselines), and how it fails — 'AI-powered' without evals is a label, not a capability.
AI-powered means it automatically learns your environment, so evaluation is unnecessary.
Ask for the CEO's AI vision statement as due diligence.
If the datasheet says AI, the product must be better than non-AI alternatives.
scenarios.why: AI claims are testable claims: evals, training data provenance, and documented failure modes separate capability from marketing. A model you cannot evaluate is a black box you are being asked to trust — and in security tooling, unmeasured 'intelligence' usually means unmeasured false positives paging your team.
scenarios.hint: Ask the vendor to show you one number that would change if the AI were removed.

scenarios.title: Negotiating the Exit Before the Entrance
scenarios.situation: You are signing a three-year SaaS deal. Legal wants termination assistance, data-return format and timeline, and renewal price protections in the contract. Sales says 'we can sort that out at renewal.'
scenarios.prompt: What are the non-negotiable contract terms?
evidence: Leverage curve
Your negotiating power is highest before signature, moderate at renewal, and near zero mid-term when you are operationally dependent.
Standard traps
Auto-renewal with uncapped uplift, vague 'industry-standard' data return, and termination assistance billed at punitive rates.
choices: Get it in writing up front: data export format and timeline, termination-assistance period with agreed rates, renewal uplift caps, and auto-renewal controls — the exit is negotiated when you still have the option to walk away.
Sign now; exit terms are easier to negotiate once you are a valued customer.
A handshake on data return is sufficient with an enterprise vendor.
Longer committed terms always reduce lock-in, so extend to five years.
scenarios.why: Every favorable exit term is bought with the credible threat of not signing. Post-signature, the vendor monetizes your switching cost instead — through uplift, egress friction, and assistance fees. Contract hygiene (portability, caps, renewal mechanics) is the cheapest lock-in insurance available.
scenarios.hint: Ask sales which of these terms gets easier to obtain after you are locked in for three years.

scenarios.title: Build, Buy, or Borrow?
scenarios.situation: Your team needs workflow automation. Options: build in-house, buy a SaaS product, or adopt an open-source project. Engineering wants to build ('we can do it better'); finance wants the cheapest sticker price.
evidence: The real question
Commodity capabilities (auth, CI, ticketing) rarely differentiate the business; engineering time spent re-building them is time not spent on what does.
Hidden costs
Build: maintenance forever. Buy: subscription plus lock-in. Borrow (open source): operations, upgrades, and security patching are yours — 'free' is a license term, not a TCO.
choices: Score each option on: is it core to the business, three-year total cost, operational burden, and exit cost — buy or borrow commodity capabilities, build only where it differentiates, and prefer open standards and portable data either way.
Always build; vendors cannot be trusted with anything.
Always buy the cheapest sticker price; engineering time is free.
Open source has no costs, so it always wins.
scenarios.why: Build-vs-buy is a portfolio decision, not an ideology: build where the capability is a differentiator you must control, buy or borrow where it is table stakes. Open source shifts cost from licenses to operations — often the right trade, but a trade nonetheless. Open standards keep every option reversible.
scenarios.hint: Ask which choice still looks good in year three, when the novelty is gone and only maintenance remains.

lessons.title: Vendor Landscape — Core concepts
concepts: Map vendors to problems before shortlisting: categorize by capability (identity, endpoint, network, data, compute) and ask what data each tool can actually observe — demos optimize for impressiveness, not fit.

Translate marketing into specifications: named ciphers and protocol versions instead of 'military-grade', evals and benchmarks instead of 'AI-powered', audit reports (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001) instead of trust-me.
Price the total over three years: licenses plus egress, API/request charges, storage tiers, operations headcount, and exit costs. The sticker price is never the total price.

Lock-in has flavors — data gravity, proprietary APIs and formats, contract terms, skill monoculture — and each needs its own mitigation: portable formats, open standards, contractual portability, and multi-vendor competence.
Read SLAs as compensation schedules, not reliability promises: do the nines math (99.9% is ~43.8 min/month), read the exclusions, and judge real reliability from incident history.

Negotiate the exit before the entrance: data-return format and timeline, termination assistance, and renewal caps belong in the contract while you can still walk away — leverage only decreases after signature.

example.code:
python3 -c "sla=0.999; print(f'Allowed downtime/month: {(1-sla)*30*24*60:.1f} minutes')"
# Allowed downtime/month: 43.2 minutes
python3 -c "sla=0.9999; print(f'Allowed downtime/month: {(1-sla)*30*24*60:.1f} minutes')"
# Allowed downtime/month: 4.3 minutes
example.walkthrough: One extra nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold — 43 minutes versus 4. Then read the SLA's exclusions and claims process, because the number alone says nothing about maintenance windows, dependency carve-outs, or who must detect and file for credits.

pitfalls: Common trap: buying from the demo — POC success in a vendor-guided trial predicts little about production operations.
Common trap: ignoring renewal mechanics — uncapped uplift and auto-renewal turn a good year-one price into a bad year-three trap.
Common trap: assuming open source means free — licenses are free, but operations, upgrades, and patching are yours.
Common trap: treating the SLA percentage as a reliability guarantee instead of doing the nines math and checking incident history.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Score Vendors on a Weighted Rubric
labs.objective: Evaluate three fictional vendors against a weighted rubric so the decision is driven by criteria, not demos.
steps: Create rubric.csv with columns criterion,weight (weights sum to 100): capability fit, security posture, total 3-year cost, data portability, support/SLA, exit cost.
Score three fictional vendors 1-5 per criterion in scores.csv, with a one-line evidence note per score (no score without evidence).
Write score.py to compute weighted totals and print a ranked table.
Run python3 score.py and record the ranking plus the single weakest criterion of the winner.
Write decision.md: the pick, the top two risks, and the contract terms that would mitigate them.

checks.hint: score.py should print each vendor's weighted total and the final ranking.

labs.title: Draft an Exit Checklist and Audit a Contract
labs.objective: Produce a reusable SaaS exit checklist and use it to audit a sample contract excerpt for lock-in traps.
steps: Create exit-checklist.md covering: data export format and timeline, API availability, termination-assistance period and rates, credential/key rotation, renewal and uplift terms, auto-renewal controls.
Save the provided sample contract excerpt as contract.txt in the workspace.
grep contract.txt for termination, data return, renewal, and fee language; log every hit with its clause number.
Mark each checklist item as covered, vague, or missing against the grep results.
Write findings.md: the three riskiest gaps and the exact redlines you would send back to the vendor.

checks.hint: grep -in for termination, data return, renewal, and uplift to surface the relevant clauses.

simulations.title: Why Did the Migration Fail?
simulations.brief: The 'lift and shift' to the new vendor's cloud failed at 70% with data locked in proprietary formats. Diagnose the lock-in.

steps.symptom: Migration stalled at 70%. Remaining data sits in the old vendor's proprietary backup format; their export tool 'is deprecated'.
evidence: Contract
No data-portability clause; export API was 'best effort'
Format
Backups in a proprietary format readable only by their appliance
Timeline
The vendor was acquired 6 months ago; support is now a chatbot
options: The migration team is too slow — add contractors
Lock-in by design: no portability clause, proprietary formats, and a deprecated export path mean exit was never actually possible — the failure was signed at procurement, not at migration
The new vendor's tooling is inadequate
steps.explain: Exit cost is set at purchase, not at exit. No portability clause + proprietary formats + deprecated exports = a roach motel. The diagnosis: procurement evaluated features and price, never the exit.

steps.symptom: You're stuck mid-migration with 30% of data hostage. What's the least-bad recovery?
evidence: Leverage
You're still paying the old vendor six figures annually
Options
Pay their 'professional services' ransom / rebuild from source systems / sue
Constraint
Business needs the data in 60 days
options: Sue for the data — principle matters

Negotiate a one-time export engagement while rebuilding critical datasets from source systems in parallel — pay the ransom once, never again, and document the cost as the case study for the new procurement policy
Abandon the 30% — it was probably stale
steps.explain: Pragmatic exit: pay the one-time export (it's cheaper than the lawsuit and faster than rebuild alone), parallel-rebuild from sources to verify, and convert the ransom invoice into the political capital for a portability-first procurement policy.

steps.symptom: New procurement policy drafted. What single clause prevents the next roach motel?
evidence: Constraint
One contractual requirement, enforceable and testable
Goal
Exit must be possible on day one, not just day 1,000
options: Data portability in open formats via a documented, tested export API — with a contractual exit-assistance obligation and the right to a trial export before signing
steps.explain: Test the exit before you enter: a trial export during evaluation proves portability is real, and the exit-assistance clause prices the vendor's cooperation. Uptime SLAs protect the stay; portability protects the leave.

simulations.debrief: Vendor failures are procurement failures: evaluate the exit with the same rigor as the features, demand open formats and tested exports, and price the ransom you never want to pay.

simulations.title: Build or Buy
simulations.brief: Your team needs a feature-flagging system. Build it in two weeks, or buy the market leader at $40k/year? Decide with TCO, not vibes.

steps.text: Feature flags needed. Build: ~2 engineer-weeks now, then maintenance forever. Buy: $40k/year, SOC 2 included, 1-day integration. Your team's roadmap is already full. Call it.

choices.label: Build — $40k/year is robbery for something so simple
choices.feedback: Simple to build, expensive to own: percentages, targeting, audit logs, kill switches, and the on-call burden — forever. The $40k was buying you out of all of it.

choices.label: Buy — run the TCO: 2 weeks build + ~0.25 FTE maintenance forever vs. $40k/year with compliance included
choices.feedback: The TCO math: 0.25 FTE at loaded cost ≈ $50k/year in maintenance alone, before the audit-log feature request arrives. Buying is cheaper AND faster.

choices.label: Build the MVP now, evaluate buying next quarter
choices.feedback: The classic hedge that becomes permanent: the MVP accrues users, migration gets scheduled 'later', and you're maintaining flags in 2029.

steps.text: You built it. Eighteen months later: the flags system needs audit logging for a compliance review, percentage rollouts are buggy, and the original author left. The 'free' system now costs real pain. What now?

choices.label: Assign the new hire to maintain it — that's what juniors are for
choices.feedback: You've converted a $40k buy decision into a permanent junior-engineer tax plus compliance risk. The TCO keeps compounding.

choices.label: Migrate to the vendor now — the 18 months proved the maintenance cost; cut losses and buy
choices.feedback: Correct late: the experiment produced data (real maintenance cost), and the data says buy. Sunk cost acknowledged, migration scheduled.

steps.text: You bought it. Year two: the vendor raises prices 40% and announces the 'enterprise tier' your features now require. The lock-in you accepted has teeth. Response?

choices.label: Pay it — switching costs more than the increase
choices.feedback: You've now ratified the price hike as strategy. Next year's increase is already being planned.

choices.label: Invoke the contract's price-cap clause you negotiated at purchase, and start the 90-day exit evaluation the contract also guarantees
choices.feedback: This is why the purchase included caps and exit rights: the cap holds this year, the credible exit threat disciplines next year's negotiation. Procurement done right.

simulations.debrief: Build vs. buy is TCO vs. TCO: loaded maintenance cost forever versus subscription plus exit rights. And every purchase negotiates the divorce (caps, portability, exit assistance) before the wedding.

simulations.title: Run the Evaluation
simulations.brief: Order the vendor evaluation process from problem definition to signed contract.

steps.context: You need a new monitoring vendor. Order the evaluation steps.
items: Define the problem and success criteria in vendor-neutral terms
Shortlist 3 vendors; run the same weighted scorecard on each
Trial the top two with real workloads — including a trial data export
Check references: ask their customers about the exit, not just the onboarding
Negotiate price caps, portability, and exit assistance — then sign

simulations.debrief: Neutral criteria first, scorecards second, trials with exit tests third, references about exits fourth, and the divorce negotiated fifth. Most teams start at step 2 and skip steps 3–5 — that's where the lock-in lives.

simulations.title: Audit the Contract
simulations.brief: A SaaS renewal contract has 3 traps. Find them before legal signs.

steps.config:
# renewal.conf — SaaS year 3
auto_renew = true, 3yr          # line 2
price_cap = none               # line 3
uplift = 15%/yr               # line 4
data_export = 'on request'      # line 5
export_format = proprietary     # line 6
sla_credits = capped 10%        # line 7
termination = 90d notice        # line 8

issues.description: Auto-renew locks 3 years with no action — the renewal happens by inertia, exactly as designed.
issues.fix: auto_renew = false; renewals require explicit approval with a market check.

issues.description: No price cap combined with 15%/yr uplift (line 4) — year-3 pricing is whatever they want.
issues.fix: price_cap = CPI+2% or 5%, whichever is lower.

issues.description: Export in proprietary format makes the 'on request' export (line 5) useless — you can leave with data you can't use.
issues.fix: export_format = open formats (CSV/Parquet/JSON) via documented API.

simulations.debrief: Lines 5, 7, 8 are workable (export on request, capped credits, 90-day notice). The traps: inertia auto-renewal, uncapped compounding uplift, and a proprietary-format export. Contracts are code for money — review them like code.

simulations.title: The Renewal Negotiation
simulations.brief: Your EDR vendor wants +35% at renewal. You have 60 days, a credible alternative, and a tired team. Negotiate.

steps.text: EDR renewal: +35%, 60 days to decide, team dreads a rip-and-replace. The vendor's rep says 'everyone's seeing adjustments.' Your opening?

choices.label: 'We'll pay it — migration is too disruptive right now.'
choices.feedback: You've negotiated against yourself. The rep just learned your threat point is zero.

choices.label: 'We've completed a trial export and a POC with your competitor. Here's our walk-away number — 5% over last year, 2-year term, price cap included.'
choices.feedback: The holy trinity: demonstrated exit (trial export), named alternative (POC done), specific terms. Now it's a negotiation.

choices.label: Go silent for 45 days to 'create pressure'
choices.feedback: Silence without a deadline is just delay. The rep waits; your 60 days shrink to 15 and the leverage inverts.

steps.text: You signaled you'll pay. The rep returns with '+30% — I fought for you.' Fifteen days left. Any recovery?

choices.label: Accept the 30% — it's better than 35%
choices.feedback: Anchoring worked exactly as designed: 35→30 feels like a win while you pay 30% more for the same product.

choices.label: Restart properly: brief procurement, run the competitive POC in the remaining 15 days, come back with the walk-away
choices.feedback: Late but real: even a compressed POC restores some leverage. Painful lesson in opening discipline.

steps.text: The rep counters: '+12%, and we'll throw in the new module free.' Your walk-away was +5% with a cap. The team is tired. Close it how?

choices.label: Take the 12% — the free module softens it and the team needs rest
choices.feedback: The 'free' module is shelfware with renewal implications. You traded 7 points for tiredness.

choices.label: '8%, 2-year, cap at 5%/yr, and the module in writing with no auto-upgrade — or we sign the competitor Friday.'
choices.feedback: Specific, final, and credible — the Friday deadline is real because the POC is done. That's how renewals close at fair prices.

simulations.debrief: Renewal leverage is manufactured before the negotiation: trial exports, completed POCs, walk-away numbers, and real deadlines. The rep's 'adjustments' meet your arithmetic — and arithmetic wins.

consoleSims.title: Compare Architectures
consoleSims.brief: Two vendors, two reference architectures. Build the neutral comparison network: VPC, subnets, security groups.

tasks.instruction: Create a VPC named 'eval-vpc' with CIDR 10.30.0.0/16.
Create a subnet in 'eval-vpc' with CIDR 10.30.1.0/24 in AZ us-east-1a.
tasks.hint: Subnets: VPC NAME eval-vpc, CIDR 10.30.1.0/24, AZ us-east-1a.

tasks.instruction: Create a security group named 'eval-sg' on 'eval-vpc'.
tasks.hint: Security Groups: VPC NAME eval-vpc, GROUP NAME eval-sg.

tasks.instruction: Add an inbound rule to 'eval-sg': tcp port 443 from 10.30.0.0/16.
tasks.hint: Add rule: SG eval-sg, PROTOCOL tcp, PORT 443, CIDR 10.30.0.0/16.

consoleSims.debrief: Evaluate vendors on neutral ground: identical reference architectures, identical rules, scorecards not slideware. The network you build for the POC is the network the decision deserves.

consoleSims.title: Score the Vendors
consoleSims.brief: Scorecards live in a database. Build the vendors table and query the weighted results.

tasks.instruction: Create the table 'vendors' with columns: id INT, name TEXT, score INT, exit_rating INT.

params.name: vendors
params.columns: id INT, name TEXT, score INT, exit_rating INT

tasks.hint: Tables: create 'vendors' with columns exactly: id INT, name TEXT, score INT, exit_rating INT.
Create index: TABLE vendors, COLUMN score.

tasks.instruction: Run a query selecting vendors ordered by score descending.
tasks.hint: Type: SELECT * FROM vendors ORDER BY score DESC; — must contain 'ORDER BY score'.

tasks.instruction: Run a query selecting vendors with exit_rating above 7 — portability matters.
tasks.hint: Type: SELECT * FROM vendors WHERE exit_rating > 7; — must contain 'exit_rating > 7'.

consoleSims.debrief: The scorecard is a database: every vendor scored on the same criteria, exit rating as a first-class column, queries instead of opinions. Decisions you can re-run are decisions you can defend.

consoleSims.title: Work the Vendor Tickets
consoleSims.brief: Vendor support runs through your queue, not their portal. Log it, assign it, track it.

tasks.instruction: Create a P2 ticket titled 'Vendor export API returning proprietary format'.

params.title: Vendor export API returning proprietary format

tasks.hint: New ticket: TITLE exactly as given, PRIORITY P2.

tasks.instruction: Add a note to INC-9001: 'Escalated to vendor TAM; SLA clock running.'

params.text: Escalated to vendor TAM; SLA clock running.

tasks.hint: Add note: INC-9001 with the exact text.

consoleSims.debrief: Vendor issues in your ticketing system means your SLA clock, your escalation path, your evidence trail. The portal is theirs; the record is yours.

consoleSims.title: Lock Down Vendor Egress
consoleSims.brief: The new vendor's agent phones home. Control exactly what it may reach with host firewall rules.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule: OUTPUT chain, tcp port 443, source 10.30.0.0/16, action ACCEPT — the agent may use HTTPS.
tasks.hint: Rules section: CHAIN OUTPUT, PROTOCOL tcp, PORT 443, SOURCE 10.30.0.0/16, ACTION ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule: OUTPUT chain, tcp port 22, source 0.0.0.0/0, action DROP — the agent may not SSH anywhere.
tasks.hint: Add rule: CHAIN OUTPUT, PROTOCOL tcp, PORT 22, SOURCE 0.0.0.0/0, ACTION DROP.

tasks.instruction: Set the default policy of the OUTPUT chain to DROP — deny by default, allow by exception.
tasks.hint: Default policies section: CHAIN OUTPUT, POLICY DROP.

consoleSims.debrief: Vendor agents get the same treatment as any third party: explicit allows, explicit denies, default-deny underneath. Trust is a firewall rule, not a feeling.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel

Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?

Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?

Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.

media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.

ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.
